edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), Ad martyres, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Sed haec exempla constantiae omittamus de affectatione venientis. Convertamur ad ipsam conditionis humanae contemplationem, ut et illa nos instruant, si qua constanter adeunda sint, quae et invitis evenire consueverunt. Quotiens enim incendia vivos cremaverunt! quotiens ferae et in silvis suis et in mediis civitatibus elapsae caveis, homines devoraverunt! quot a latronibus fetro, ab hostibus etiam cruce extincti sunt, torti prius, imo et omni contumelia expuncti! Nemo non etiam hominis caussa pati potest, quod in caussa Dei pati dubitat. Ad hoc quidem vel praesentia nobis tempora documenta sint, quantae qualesque personae inopinatos, natalibus, et dignitatibus, et corporibus, et aetatibus suis, exitus referunt, hominis caussa: aut ab ipso, si contra eum fecerint: aut ab adversariis ejus, si pro eo steterint.
pass_a_gloss: But let us omit these examples of constancy from affectation of what is coming. Let us turn to the very contemplation of the human condition, so that those things also may instruct us, if some things are to be undertaken constantly, which even to the unwilling are accustomed to happen. For how many times have fires burned alive! how many times have wild beasts, both in their own woods and having escaped from cages in the midst of cities, devoured men! how many have been killed by robbers with a chain, by enemies even with a cross, having been tortured first, indeed even having been afflicted with every insult! No one is not able to suffer even for the sake of a man, what he doubts to suffer for the sake of God. For this, indeed, even the present times are lessons for us, how many and what kind of persons, with their own births, and dignities, and bodies, and ages, bring about unexpected outcomes, for the sake of a man: either by him, if they have acted against him: or by his adversaries, if they have stood for him.
pass_b_english: We should skip these examples of constancy born of showmanship about what is coming. Let us turn instead to the very contemplation of the human condition so that these things, too, may instruct us, if there are any things that must be faced steadfastly—things that are accustomed to happen even to the unwilling. How many times have fires burned people alive! How many times have wild beasts, both in their own woods and after escaping from cages in the middle of cities, devoured men! How many have been killed by robbers with a chain, by enemies even with a cross—tortured first, indeed even afflicted with every insult! No one is unable to suffer even for the sake of a mere human being what he hesitates to suffer for the sake of God. Indeed, the present times themselves serve as lessons for us: how many and what kind of persons bring about unexpected outcomes, for the sake of a man—either by him, if they have acted against him, or by his adversaries, if they have stood for him—regardless of their own births, dignities, bodies, and ages.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass B correctly handles the complex syntax of the final sentence, where the list of attributes (natalibus, et dignitatibus, et corporibus, et aetatibus suis) modifies the 'persons' (personae) who bring about the outcomes, whereas Pass A follows the Latin word order more literally but slightly less clearly in English. Both preserve the meaning of 'fetro' as 'chain' (though 'fetro' is a known OCR/textual variant for 'funiculo' or similar in some editions, the translation is consistent with the provided text).
